title: Self-reports vs. web-browsing: a multiverse analysis of media use comparison regarding timeframe, media use types, and web-browsing data pre-processing strategies
authors: Milin Zhang, Emese Domahidi

title: Longitudinal Associations Between Problematic Internet Use Components and Adolescents’ Quality of Life
authors: Román Ronzón-Tirado, Joaquin Manuel González-Cabrera, Juan Manuel Machimbarrena, Esther Calvete
abstract: Although problematic Internet use (PIU) has been increasingly associated with poorer health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in adolescents, longitudinal evidence examining the longitudinal associations between specific PIU components and HRQoL remains limited. Guided by the cognitive–behavioral model of PIU, this study investigated the longitudinal relationships between four PIU components (preference for online social interaction, mood regulation, deficient self-regulation, and negative consequences) and HRQoL across three time points. The sample comprised 2,616 Spanish adolescents. A random intercept cross-lagged panel model was employed to disentangle between-person from within-person associations between variables. At the between-person level, all PIU components were positively interrelated and negatively associated with HRQoL. At the within-person level, only deficits in self-regulation preceded subsequent increases in mood regulation. Additionally, deficits in self-regulation were the only PIU component to precede decreases in HRQoL over time. Bidirectional associations were also observed, as declines in HRQoL preceded worsening self-regulation deficits and negative consequences. These findings highlight the role of self-regulation deficits in PIU and their association with adolescent well-being, underscoring the importance of targeting self-regulation processes in prevention and intervention efforts.

title: Does Fear of Missing Out Precede Problematic Internet Use, or the Reverse? A Two-Wave Cross-Lagged Study of Taiwanese Adolescents
authors: Chi-Jung Sui, Mingchuan Hsieh, Ming-Hsueh Tsai
abstract: Fear of missing out (FOMO), online social comparison, and problematic Internet use (PIU) are consistently correlated in adolescents, and influential models treat FOMO as a motivational antecedent of problematic use. This temporal ordering, however, has rarely been tested against its reverse. We analyzed the first two annual waves of the Taiwan i-Generation Panel Study ( N = 8,311; Grade 7 to Grade 8; 49 percent girls) and estimated a latent cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) of PIU symptoms, FOMO, and online social comparison, using the survey weights and jackknife replicate standard errors. PIU symptoms predicted later FOMO (standardized β = 0.12, p < 0.001), and FOMO predicted later PIU ( β = 0.06, p = 0.017). The difference between the two directions was not statistically significant (Δ β = 0.06, 95 percent confidence interval [−0.01, 0.12], p = 0.093), and this remained so across eight analytic specifications, in which the estimates varied depending on the measurement model. FOMO and social comparison also predicted each other in the primary model but not in the ordinal sensitivity analyses, whereas social comparison did not predict later PIU, and all cross-lagged associations were small. These prospective associations do not support treating FOMO only as an antecedent of problematic use, because problematic use also preceded FOMO. A two-wave design cannot separate within-person change from stable differences between adolescents, so the findings describe prospective associations and await replication across three or more waves.

title: Fostering constructive online news discussions: The role of anonymity and subjectivity in shaping perceived polarization in a Dutch sample of online commenters
authors: Carla Anne Roos, Sara Bögels, Emiel Krahmer
journal_full: Cyberpsychology: Journal of Psychosocial Research on Cyberspace
abstract: Online news discussions are often characterized by polarization and hostile interactions, which may discourage people from participating. This study examines whether two features of online comments influence how people perceive the polarization and disinhibition of commenters, as well as people’s own willingness to join discussions: sender anonymity and subjective phrasing, that is, explicitly phrasing an opinion as an opinion (e.g., “I think”, “In my opinion”). We conducted an experiment with a purposive subsample drawn from a representative general population sample of Dutch adults who self-reported to be currently or previously active in online news discussions (N = 294; repeated-measures, age range = 17–88 years). Participants evaluated manipulated comments to news articles about issues that were generally considered polarized in Dutch society. Sender anonymity did not affect perceived polarization, perceived disinhibition, or intentions to participate in discussions. Subjectivity, however, led participants to perceive comments as less polarized and less disinhibited. Although this did not increase participants’ intentions to join discussions, participants themselves used more subjective language when replying to subjectively phrased comments. These findings suggest that subtle changes in the way opinions are expressed can shape interaction norms in online discussions. Subjective phrasing may encourage more constructive communication styles to spread between users, even without top-down moderation or requirements for identity disclosure.

title: Basic psychological need satisfaction and problematic gaming, mobile phone use, and social networking in adolescents: Disentangling between- and within-person associations
authors: Xuan Xu, Haide Chen, Wan Zhao, Lingfeng Gao
journal_full: Cyberpsychology: Journal of Psychosocial Research on Cyberspace
abstract: Basic psychological need satisfaction is often treated as a dynamic antecedent and consequence of adolescents’ problematic use of digital technologies. However, longitudinal associations may reflect stable differences between adolescents rather than changes occurring within the same adolescent. Using three-wave data from 1,024 Chinese adolescents assessed at six-month intervals, this study estimated multiple-indicator latent random-intercept cross-lagged panel models examining psychological need satisfaction in relation to Internet gaming disorder (IGD), problematic mobile phone use (PMPU), and social networking site addiction (SNSA) scores. At the between-person level, lower need satisfaction was associated with higher IGD, r = −.442, 95% CI [−.783, −.102], and PMPU, r = −.614, 95% CI [−.952, −.277]. The association with SNSA was negative but not statistically significant, r = −.431, 95% CI [−.926, .064]. None of the six-month cross-lagged paths was statistically significant. In dimension-specific models, FDR-adjusted between-person associations remained for competence and relatedness with IGD and PMPU, whereas none of the dimension-specific cross-lagged paths was statistically significant. Composite-score and classroom-cluster-robust analyses yielded the same general pattern. These findings refine the theoretical interpretation of the need and technology use association: At a six-month timescale, the clearest detected pattern was stable covariation between adolescents, whereas reciprocal cross-lagged within-person associations were not detected. Distinguishing these levels provides a more precise basis for separating enduring need-related vulnerability from shorter-term compensatory processes.

title: Users vs. independent judges: Comparing perceived authorship and ownership in AI-supported collaborative writing
authors: Joseph Fung, Kamryn Kadotani, Samantha McMichael, Virginia Kwan
journal_full: Cyberpsychology: Journal of Psychosocial Research on Cyberspace
abstract: With the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in academic and creative settings, understanding how this technology impacts fundamental concepts of authorship and ownership is important to protect learning, maintain academic integrity, and establish clear policies. This study (N = 320; 18 to 44 years old, M = 19.55, SD = 2.39) utilized a 2 (user vs independent judge) x 4 (completely user generated; AI-generated and user edited 4 sentences; user chooses from 3 AI-generated options; completely AI generated) between-subjects design to examine how levels of Large Language Model (LLM) input affect attributions of authorship and ownership by both the users and the independent judges in a collaborative writing task. Findings reveal a significant inverse relationship between the level of LLM input and users’ reported ownership and authorship and a positive relationship between their attributions of ownership and authorship. Additionally, discrepancies emerged between users’ and judges’ attributions, particularly at high and low levels of LLM input, suggesting that third-party evaluators and users may use different factors in allocating credit. Furthermore, this research investigated the role of background factors such as users’ experience with AI, their attitudes toward AI, and their writing level in moderating the relationships between (1) AI input level and attributions of ownership and (2) attributions of ownership and authorship. The findings reveal the need to identify optimal levels of AI integration that support learning without diminishing students’ sense of authorship and to develop assessment strategies that address differences in attributions of ownership by users and independent judges. For policy, the observed differences in attribution demonstrate the complexities of assigning credit and responsibility in AI-assisted creative works.

title: Is Europe tuning out? Selective news avoidance and low news consumption across 15 countries in the European Parliament elections
authors: Svenja Schäfer, Sanne Tamboer, Sanne Kruikemeier, Rens Vliegenthart, Alice Hamilton, Annelien Van Remoortere, Susan Vermeer
abstract: Keeping up with the news is essential for democracy, particularly around elections when citizens make voting decisions. However, in secondary elections like those for the European Parliament (EP), individuals often actively avoid election news or engage with it minimally. We surveyed 15 European countries before the 2024 EP elections ( N = 7633) to examine types of news avoidance, news consumption, and their individual- and country-level predictors. Findings reveal regional patterns: low news consumption is most prevalent in Northern Europe, while selective avoidance is more common in Southern and Eastern Europe. Country-level factors play a minimal role, with most variance explained at the individual level. Selective avoidance is linked to low interest and dissatisfaction with news coverage, while low news consumption is associated with lower interest and perceived EU competence. This suggests different types of news avoidance require tailored approaches to foster engagement with EP election news.

title: Beyond the Barrier of the Eco-Warrior
authors: Roseline van Gogh
abstract: Abstract: Media portrayals of eco-friendly people often display highly devoted eco-warriors. Although such portrayals may appeal to niche audiences, they make eco-friendly people appear distant and unrelatable to many others. Among young adults, highly devoted eco-warriors are admired for their dedication, yet frequently associated with negative traits, such as being pushy or judgmental. As these negative traits have become part of young adults’ existing cognitive schema of eco-friendly people (i.e., green people schema), they hesitate to identify with this group. Drawing on schema theory, this study investigates if media portrayals of eco-friendly people that challenge this narrow schema (i.e., schema-incongruent portrayals) improve young adults’ green people schema, and in turn, their eco-friendly group identity. In an online scenario-based experiment ( N = 174) using a one-factor mixed factorial design, participants saw Instagram portrayals of eco-friendly people that either confirmed or challenged the existing schema of highly devoted eco-warriors, representing the schema-congruent and schema-incongruent condition respectively. Results show that young adults’ green people schema only improved from pre-exposure to postexposure in the schema-incongruent condition. More specifically, young adults attributed fewer negative traits to eco-friendly people after seeing schema-incongruent (vs. schema-congruent) Instagram portrayals. This, in turn, related to stronger group identification. When young adults’ environmental self-identity was taken into account, the indirect effect of schema-incongruent portrayals on group identification through the green people schema was no longer significant, hinting that the effectiveness of schema-incongruent portrayals may depend on how eco-friendly individuals perceive themselves.

title: Who Engages More, How, and Where? Examining Social Disparities in Multiplatform Social Media News Use Across Forty-Four Societies
authors: Macau K. F. Mak, Michelle Le He, Leon Zhenglang Wang
abstract: As more individuals adopt multiple social media platforms for news engagement, this study examines whether, how, and where sociodemographic disparities in multiplatform news use arise. Analyzing data from 2024, we find that women, older, less-educated, and low-income individuals use fewer platforms for news. Yet these disparities differ in nature: some groups adopt fewer platforms in general, others are less likely to use social media for news, and some experience both. Platform-level analyses largely mirror these patterns. Press freedom, polarization, and populism further shape these disparities. Robustness checks with data from earlier waves indicate that many patterns have persisted since 2018.

title: Imagining the World Through News: A Cross-National Analysis of Country-Based Issue Ownership Networks
authors: Zhuoyu Wang, Lei Guo, Mengmeng Wu, Chris J. Vargo
abstract: This study examines how news media in different countries imagine the world and what accounts for cross-national similarity in these mediated worldviews. We introduce Country-based Issue Ownership Networks (CIONs), which conceptualize world imagination as associations between countries and issues in international news coverage. Drawing on 4,471,278 news articles from 42 countries, we construct two-mode country–issue networks and reveal their relational structure. We find a shared global foundation and three distinct communities of worldview. Economic interdependence is the dominant predictor of CION similarity, suggesting that cross-national world imagination is shaped primarily by a material logic.

title: Ports of illiberalism: Cross-platform diffusion of far right, conspiratorial, and reactionary Rumble videos on Facebook
authors: Fatima Gaw, Chloe R. Mortenson, Hoda Fakhari, Rod Abhari, Inaya Fatima Hussain, Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Erik C. Nisbet
abstract: Alt-tech platforms like Rumble are a critical part of the illiberal public sphere where extremist and ideological communities converge. Despite their seeming isolation, alt-tech content penetrates big-tech platforms through parallel ports—socio-technical conduits that promote illiberal politics among mainstream audiences. This study develops an expanded typology of parallel ports based on their differentiated roles in cross-platform diffusion and applies it to the actor network sharing Rumble video links on Facebook. Using content and network analysis, it traces the systematic sharing of the most engaged Rumble video links from 2022 to 2023, identifying the actors and communities that sustain the Rumble–Facebook pipeline. Findings show that primary ports drive social media engagement while horizontal peripheral ports maintain ideological cohesion as central actors in the co-sharing network. Vertical peripheral ports, while less central, provide upward amplification. We discuss how alt-tech illiberal content penetrates big-tech platforms and its evolution as platform content moderation weakens.

title: Conspirative nudge: Visual dynamics, far-right engagement, and alt-tech infrastructures on Telegram during Brazil’s 2022 election day
authors: Elias C. Bitencourt, Paulo F. C. Fonseca, Eurico Matos, Letícia Cesarino, Leonardo F. Nascimento
abstract: This study investigates how images circulated in Brazilian far-right Telegram groups during the 2022 presidential runoff. Combining transformer-based computer-vision clustering with qualitative analysis, we analysed 5,384 unique images within 78,032 visual messages across 373 public groups and channels, derived from an initial data set of 126,640 messages collected during election day. We identified four interconnected dynamics – synchronization of informational flows, segmented emotional mobilization, epistemic legitimacy fabrication, and creation of cross-platform repositories – that anchor visual practices within Telegram’s alt-tech infrastructure. These dynamics configure a sociotechnical environment we conceptualize as a conspirative nudge: a latent, distributed state of affairs that facilitates emergence of conspiratorial practices by rendering certain interpretations more temporally aligned, affectively resonant, and visually actionable. Our framework extends debates in political communication and platform studies by foregrounding how platform affordances and visual artefacts jointly enact conspiratorial environments beyond deliberate intervention.

title: Mirror worlds and misogyny: A mixed-methods analysis of incel discourse across mainstream and alt-tech platforms
authors: Karmvir K Padda
abstract: This article analyzes incel discourse as both an affective and ideological system across mainstream and alt-tech platforms, specifically Reddit and Incels.is. Drawing on a Computational Grounded Theory approach, I combine BERTopic modeling with qualitative thematic discourse analysis to examine how incel communities convert despair, humiliation, and rage into epistemic claims about gender, power, and justice. The analysis identifies three recurring formations: biologized rejection, the “foid” logic, and glorified violence, which persist across platforms despite stark differences in moderation and visibility. Building on Naomi Klein’s theory of the Mirror World, I argue that alt-tech spaces do not invent new ideologies but stabilize, intensify, and ritualize misogynistic extremism. Incel discourse is not merely descriptive; it is productive, ontologizing emotional pain and transforming grievance into knowledge through repetition, resonance, and digital infrastructures. Conceptualized as an affective epistemology, this system shows how misogyny is foundational, making violence feel not only imaginable but morally justified.

title: Prevalence or Threat? How Misinformation Interventions Shape Veracity Discernment and Trust in Scientists
authors: Myojung Chung, S. Mo Jones-Jang, Betty S. Lai
abstract: Science misinformation poses two distinct problems: promoting inaccurate scientific beliefs and undermining trust in scientists. Yet little research has examined the psychological mechanisms through which interventions may address both problems. An experiment ( N = 832) compared accuracy prompts and threat-focused and efficacy-focused forewarning, examining perceived misinformation prevalence and threat as mediators. Both forewarning messages increased perceived prevalence and threat, but only threat was associated with better veracity discernment and greater trust in scientists. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing how widespread misinformation seems from how harmful it feels when examining how interventions shape veracity discernment and trust in scientists.

title: Correctness Costs Credibility? The Emotional Loop in AI-Powered Fact-Checking
authors: Wenbo Zhao, Jingtai Tang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for fact-checking, but the role of emotion in this process remains unclear. We propose an Emotional Loop in LLM-based fact-checking, in which the emotional cues in user prompts influence model responses, while the emotional tone of those responses shapes users’ subsequent evaluations. Across three studies, we examine this process in the context of partially false claims. Study 1 audits four widely accessible LLMs across 24,000 responses and shows that emotional prompts—especially negative ones—can improve LLMs’ accuracy in identifying partially false claims while also increasing the emotional intensity of their outputs. Studies 2 and 3 ( N = 400 and 299, respectively) examine how users evaluate emotionally framed LLM fact-checks. Across both studies, these evaluations depended on users’ own emotions. In particular, negatively toned replies undermined perceived credibility among users experiencing negative emotion. Together, these findings reveal what we term a “correctness costs credibility” paradox in the Emotional Loop: Emotional input can sharpen fact-checking judgments, while emotional spillover into model output may reduce perceived credibility under certain conditions. The Emotional Loop offers a process account of how emotion operates throughout artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated verification, highlighting the importance of considering both model performance and user reception in LLM-based fact-checking.

title: The Promises and Limits of Solutions Journalism: How Controversy Conditions Effects on Emotions and Attitudes in Response to News About Climate Change
authors: Adam Shehata, Kim Andersen, Mats Ekström, Emil Östlund
abstract: This study addresses an argument not considered in previous research on solutions journalism: that the emotional and attitudinal effects of solutions-focused news stories depend on the level of controversy of the solutions presented. Across two identically designed experiments focusing on reducing emissions from meat production (Study 1) and transportation (Study 2), we find that the promises of solutions journalism are conditioned by the real-world sociopolitical context in which it is embedded. Both levels of controversy and political predispositions among news consumers condition the effects of solutions journalism on the audience, even generating evidence of backfiring effects.

title: Uncertain Performance: How to Quantify Uncertainty and Draw Test Sets When Evaluating Classifiers
authors: Francisco Tomas-Valiente
abstract: Supervised machine learning has become increasingly popular in social science research, often employing classifiers to measure political constructs. Although evaluating classifiers on a test set is critical for establishing their validity, guidance on how to conduct such evaluation is limited. In particular, researchers have paid insufficient attention to the variance of performance metrics estimated on test sets. This article demonstrates that typically sized test sets yield highly noisy and often uninformative estimates of classifier performance, particularly for imbalanced tasks—common in social science applications like identifying hateful or emotional speech—where one outcome class is rare. To address this issue, this article introduces methods to quantify uncertainty in performance estimates based on their sampling distribution and validated with simulations. It also introduces a design-based approach in political science to enhance statistical precision when evaluating classifiers: efficient stratified sampling based on the outcome’s predicted probability. Simulations using synthetic and real data show that this strategy meaningfully reduces the variance of performance estimates, especially in imbalanced tasks, while ensuring that they remain consistent. Finally, the article illustrates how to calculate the test set size required to achieve a desired level of statistical precision. Accompanying statistical software enables researchers to easily implement these methods.

title: Correcting Bias When Using Latent Regressors
authors: Connor Jerzak, Stephen Jessee
abstract: Many core concepts in political science are latent and therefore can only be measured with error. Measurement error in a predictor attenuates slope coefficient estimates in regression, often biasing them toward zero. We show that widely used strategies for correcting attenuation bias—including instrumental variables and the method of composition—are themselves biased when applied to latent regressors, often performing worse than simple regression ignoring the measurement error altogether. We derive a correlation-based correction using split-sample measurement strategies. Rather than assuming a particular estimation strategy for the latent trait, our approach is modular and can be easily deployed with a wide variety of latent-variable measurement strategies, including additive score, factor or machine-learning models; it requires no joint estimation while yielding consistent slopes under standard assumptions. Simulations and applications show stronger relationships after our correction, sometimes by as much as 50%. Open-source software implements the procedure. Results underscore that latent predictors demand tailored error correction; otherwise, conventional practice can exacerbate bias.

title: Quality Controls Can Improve the Replicability of Survey Experiments Using Online Nonprobability Panels
authors: Edgar Cook, James Martherus, Alexander Podkul, Anja Kilibarda
abstract: Scholars across multiple disciplines have documented challenges related to replicability, often referred to as a “replication crisis.” While a range of explanations exist, some have argued that the growing reliance on online nonprobability samples contributes to replication failures. At the same time, concerns have mounted regarding the quality of these samples, as inattentive, duplicate, or fraudulent respondents can bias estimates and diminish effect sizes. In this research note, we replicate three well-known survey experiments, using data collected from three separate online nonprobability panels (N = 6,000). We compare the “off-the-shelf” samples with subsets that pass a series of attention and fraud checks and that remove duplicate respondents. We find that all three experiments replicate in terms of direction and significance across the full samples, but in two out of three cases, effect magnitudes are replicated only once low-quality responses are removed.

title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
authors: Thomas H. Costello, Nathaniel Rabb, Michael Nicholas Stagnaro, Gordon Pennycook, David G. Rand
journal_full: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here, we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, US adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1,042) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multiturn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found suggestive evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in some—but not all—analyses of different conspiratorial beliefs 1 to 2 mo later. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, information-focused LLM interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

title: Humans show limited ability to distinguish human-authored from AI-generated political content on social media
authors: Sejin Paik, Tiago Ventura, Rebecca Ansell, Leticia Bode, Autumn Toney-Wails, Lisa Singh
journal_full: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: This study employs a set of behavioral experiments to examine how individuals perceive the humanness of social media posts about the 2024 U.S. presidential debate between Kamala Harris and Donald Trump. Posts presented in the experiment were authored either by humans or chatbots, varying the large language model (LLM), the model architecture, the social media platform, and the political personas. Participants judged randomly paired posts to identify which they perceived to be AI-generated. We find that human-authored posts were on average perceived as more human-like than AI outputs generated from five of the six LLMs in this study. However, participants’ ability to detect AI-generated content is limited. They do so only slightly above chance in human–AI pairs, and this ability weakens for newer LLMs, varies by platform, and reflects partisan bias. Only posts generated with Llama 3.3 scored, on average, higher on perceived humanness than human-authored posts. The social media platform also mattered, with participants distinguishing human from AI on most platforms (YouTube, TikTok, Truth Social), but not on X/Twitter. Incivility and negative emotions are associated with high humanness perceptions, and partisan identity also shaped evaluations, with Republican respondents more likely to view ideologically misaligned AI posts as AI-generated.
